items.title: Family rift reaches court 🫣
items.content:
🗓️ Morning, folks! ☀️

Gold Spot, the bright orange fizzy drink that ruled Indian childhoods in the 1980s and 1990s, is making a comeback after 26 years off the shelves.

Coca-Cola is planning to relaunch the nostalgic favourite, possibly in a low-sugar or no-sugar version, with reports suggesting it could be sold in cans through quick-commerce platforms.

The hype: for an entire generation, Gold Spot was more than just an orange soda. There were collectible bottle caps, catchy jingles, beachside bottles and the iconic “The Zing Thing” campaign.

It was practically the Diet Coke of its time, except people loved it for all that sugary, tangy goodness. Now, bringing it back without much of that sugar could be quite the nostalgia test.

Markets made a strong comeback on Wednesday, with both Sensex and Nifty gaining over 1% to close at nine-month highs, recovering all of Monday’s losses.

The rally was driven by heavy buying in private banks, particularly HDFC Bank and ICICI Bank, pushing the Nifty Bank index up over 2%.

FMCG emerged as the top-performing sector, while the IT index gained 1%.

💡Spotlight: Tariff pe tariff ❌

The US is considering a fresh round of tariffs on India and 15 other major trading partners, including China, Japan, South Korea and the European Union.

The move follows an investigation into what Washington calls industrial overcapacity.

Simply put, the US believes these countries are producing more goods with government support helping their companies sell them at cheaper prices and making it harder for American manufacturers to compete.

The investigation, launched on March 11 under Section 301 of the US Trade Act, 1974, could allow Washington to impose additional duties on their exports.

For India, this could make goods exported to the US more expensive, putting Indian businesses at a disadvantage.

It could also complicate the ongoing India-US trade deal negotiations, as New Delhi is seeking lower tariffs than competing exporters such as Vietnam and Bangladesh.

Let’s hit it! 💪🏻

1 Big Thing: TVS family feud reaches the courtroom ⚖️

We are witnessing a very Indian version of Succession, as Lakshmi Venu has moved the Madras High Court seeking her share of the TVS family wealth.

The dispute covers family interests held through trusts and other ownership structures in businesses such as TVS Holdings, TVS Motor Company, TVS Credit Services and Sundaram-Clayton.

Who’s who: the dispute involves four members of the TVS family, with father Venu Srinivasan and son Sudarshan Venu on one side, and mother Mallika Srinivasan and daughter Lakshmi Venu on the other.

A quick rewind: in 2020, the larger TVS family underwent a restructuring, under which different businesses were allocated to different branches of the family.

In March 2024, the four members of Venu Srinivasan’s immediate family signed another agreement. And that’s where the disagreement lies.

  • The father and son’s side: the family settlement has already been reached.

  • The mother and daughter’s side: the agreement primarily covered trademarks, brand usage and restrictions on competing businesses. It did not divide the family wealth.

What’s happening now: on November 16, Lakshmi sent a legal notice to her father demanding a fair division of the assets. With no resolution, she has now approached the court. She has also sought access to documents that she claims were withheld despite repeated requests.

Note: Lakshmi has clarified that the dispute is about family wealth and not how these companies are run. However, the court’s decision could have implications for their indirect ownership.

The Madras High Court is likely to hear the matter on Friday.

Share

2. WeFast gets a buyer 💸

Shadowfax Tech has acquired WeFast (Borzo India) for ₹23.3 crore as it expands into on-demand goods transport within cities. The deal includes Borzo’s India delivery software and the rights to use the Borzo and WeFast names in India.

WeFast operates in more than five cities. Its network of over 32,000 delivery partners completes more than 1.2 crore deliveries a year. The company reported around ₹200 crore in adjusted revenue in 2025.

The deets: the deal gives Shadowfax access to WeFast’s local delivery network and customer base. Shadowfax plans to combine its technology and delivery network with WeFast’s operations to serve shop owners, distributors and individuals.

The move adds on-demand goods transport to a logistics platform that already handles express parcels and hyperlocal fulfilment.

The big picture: every day, thousands of vehicles move goods within Indian cities and towns. Together, they make up a $15 billion intra-city logistics market that keeps local businesses running.

As small and medium-sized businesses expand, demand for local goods transport is also growing.

In more deals,

Jupiter Wagons hit 20% as it entered into a joint venture with South Korea’s Woojin Industrial Systems. Jupiter will hold an 80% stake in the venture.

Jupiter Wagons shares hit the 20% upper circuit after the company announced a joint venture with South Korea’s Woojin Industrial Systems

Woojin has supplied around 2,200 coaches to South Korean operators, including Seoul Metro, Korea Railroad Corporation (KORAIL) and Busan Transportation Corporation. It has also supplied rolling stock and rail systems to other countries.

The why: the joint venture marks Jupiter’s entry into the metro coach and propulsion businesses.

Over the past few years, wagon and component manufacturers have branched out into propulsion systems, complete trainsets and coaches as more advanced trains like the Vande Bharat enter service in India.

3. Stocks that kept us interested 🚀

What went up ⬆️

💸 NSE rose 5% after ICICI Securities initiated coverage on the stock with a bullish outlook and ‘buy’ rating.

📈 PB Fintech and Turtlemint gained 5% after IRDAI formed a panel to review proposed changes to insurance distribution and commissions.

😮‍💨 L&T jumped around 2% after it secured an order for a 300 MW/900 MWh battery storage project in Gujarat.

💪🏻 Infosys jumped 2%, leading Nifty IT and ranking among the top gainers on the Nifty 50, which rose nearly 2%.

😋 Cipla went up 2% after it launched the first USFDA-approved Flovent HFA generic, targeting a market estimated at $350 million.

What went down ⬇️

😑 APL Apollo Tubes tumbled 11% after brokerages downgraded shares and cut targets 44% following Tata Steel’s deal.

🔻Shares of copper-related companies remained under pressure as copper prices fell, with KEI Industries among the losers after dropping nearly 4%.

What else are we snackin’ 🍿

🥐 Bakery expansion: Bikaji Foods entered the premium bakery segment with its European-inspired brand Mahè, supported by a manufacturing facility in Karnataka.

✈️ Price trends: India’s air passenger service prices surged 35.5% in Q2 FY27, while securities transaction prices fell 6.9%, according to government data.

🛒 Leadership change: Flipkart CEO Kalyan Krishnamurthy is set to step down, with Chief Product and Technology Officer Balaji Thiagarajan taking over as interim CEO until a permanent successor is announced.

💼 Finance deal: Wipro secured a finance transformation deal with BP, under which it will absorb around 3,000 employees and deploy AI and automation to improve financial operations.

That’s a wrap! Don’t let the weekday blues get to you.

items.title: Jensen’s second innings sends Nvidia soaring 🏏
items.content:
🗓️ Morning, folks! ☀️

It’s the post GTA VI world y’all and the spillover effects are coming for the city of dreams.

Mumbai’s gaming cafés are seeing a massive rush, with PS5 consoles booked back-to-back for six-hour gaming marathons and gamers waiting up to 30 minutes to play. Cafés have hiked hourly rental rates by 50%, from ₹200 to ₹300, and are reportedly recovering their GTA 6 investment within 1-2 weeks.

But there’s a larger story here. With gaming hardware becoming increasingly expensive as the AI boom drives up chip demand, buying a ₹50,000 console or a PC worth lakhs just to play a game isn’t everyone’s cup of tea.

From games to numbers 🔢,

The Sensex and Nifty recorded their biggest one-day falls in nearly five months on Monday as investors sold shares to cash in on recent gains.

IT stocks bucked the trend, with the Nifty IT index rising 1.7%. Metal and public-sector bank stocks fell the most, with their indices dropping 3.7% and 3.3%, respectively.

💡 Spotlight: Bottled water under fire 💧

Bisleri is facing legal action from India’s food safety regulator, the FSSAI.

This comes after a water sample from its Goa factory reportedly showed bromate levels above the permitted limit of 10 micrograms per litre.

Bromate is a chemical that can form during water purification. Long-term exposure to high levels may damage kidney cells and DNA, and increase cancer risk. The tricky part? Bromate has no taste, smell or colour, so you cannot detect it yourself.

Bisleri has disputed the findings, saying five of the six samples collected by the FSSAI met safety standards. It claims further tests by two laboratories found bromate within the permitted limit.

Let’s hit it! 💪🏻

1 Big Thing: Nvidia’s Jensen-free trial lasted 11 days ⏳

In what could be one of corporate America’s shortest CEO exits, Nvidia has reinstated Jensen Huang as president and CEO.

The return came only 11 days after Huang resigned and six days after Nvidia’s board publicly said it did not intend to bring him back.

The deets: as per the company, it received input from senior US government officials before concluding that his return “poses no national security risk.”

Nvidia shares surged more than 30% after the announcement as investors welcomed the return of the man who built the company into the centre of the AI boom.

How did we get here: on November 12, Huang resigned after reports concerning extramarital relationships.

One reported relationship involved Alice Huang, an unrelated former Megaspeed executive whom US authorities reportedly suspected of links to Chinese intelligence. China denied the allegation.

Another report alleged that Huang had a relationship with an Nvidia employee who reported to him.

Huang acknowledged being unfaithful to his wife. However, no public finding has established that he knowingly shared company secrets or sensitive US information.

Thousands of people identifying themselves as Nvidia employees had supported a petition demanding Huang’s return. Investors also questioned whether Nvidia could quickly replace his technical knowledge, customer relationships and influence across Silicon Valley and Washington.

Trump’s role: the US President said he intervened “directly and indirectly” with Nvidia’s board. He claimed that government investigators found no evidence that Huang personally committed any wrongdoing linked to national security.

Share

2. Brookfield puts AI on bottle duty 🏭

Brookfield has agreed to buy India’s PGP Glass from funds managed by Blackstone for $1.7 billion.

PGP says it makes one in every three nail polish bottles worldwide. It also makes glass packaging for perfumes, medicines, food and drinks. Its three factories in India and Sri Lanka supply brands in over 70 countries.

Why is Brookfield buying: the brand is paying PGP to design that shape, make the mold and get the finish right. That leaves more profit per sale than ordinary glass, according to Brookfield.

The timing helps, too. Higher costs have pushed some glassmakers in Europe and North America to cut back. Their customers still need bottles. Brookfield sees a chance for PGP to win those orders, particularly in the US and Canada.

The AI bit: Brookfield wants AI to help PGP spot shifts like that and plan what to make next. It also wants to catch faults earlier.

PGP has already seen what a difference that can make as in an earlier project with Microsoft, workers used sensors to find where bottles were going wrong on the line. Defects fell 5%.

Zoom out: Brookfield is looking beyond PGP Glass and eyeing more investment opportunities in India, the company told Mint.

The firm is particularly keen on Indian companies that cater to global markets, with PGP Glass being a prime example of the kind of investments it wants to make more of.

Share

3. Trouble brews for IndusInd Bank ♨️

IndusInd Bank fell nearly 4% after the lender formally terminated the employment of former managing director and CEO Sumant Kathpalia following an inquiry into its derivatives accounting discrepancies.

What happened: the bank moved to cut or cancel Kathpalia’s unpaid bonuses and recover some payments already made, using rules known as malus and clawback.

The action follows accounting errors revealed in March 2025 involving financial contracts tied to currencies and interest rates.

A quick rewind: the bank initially estimated that the discrepancies would affect around 2.35% of its net worth and appointed external investigators.

Incorrect accounting of certain internal derivatives transactions had overstated profits by around ₹1,960 crore. Beyond the financial impact, the issue raised questions about how the errors had gone undetected.

Why action is being taken now: although Kathpalia had resigned as MD and CEO, the bank subsequently suspended him on June 18, 2025, and continued disciplinary proceedings.

A former Bombay High Court judge conducted the inquiry and submitted the report on November 18, 2026. Two days later, the board decided to terminate his employment and invoke the provisions relating to his pay.

Share

4. Stocks that kept us interested 🚀

What went up ⬆️

💥 Premier Explosives jumped more than 6% after bagging an export order worth ₹311 crore for defence explosives.

🛣️ Ashoka Buildcon gained more than 5% after securing projects worth over ₹4,200 crore from NHAI and Rajasthan Metro.

☀️ Sterling & Wilson won three domestic orders worth over ₹2,050 crore, stock up more than 4%.

💎 Kalyan Jewellers ended more than 2% higher on news of ₹2,000-crore fundraising talks with Warburg Pincus and other PE firms.

What went down ⬇️

💊 Marksans Pharma fell over 4% after being issued a Form 483 by the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA).

🤝 APL Apollo slipped more than 20% after Tata Steel’s board approved the acquisition of a controlling stake in the company. Meanwhile, Tata Steel fell more than 8% as investors assessed the impact of the buyout.

What else are we snackin’ 🍿

🤝 Neighbourly ties: India and Nepal signed 8 deals across healthcare, space technology, urban development, agriculture and capacity building, with India also announcing ₹15,000 crore in development assistance to Nepal.

🖥️ Deal done: L&T secured a ₹2,500-5,000 crore deal to deploy NVIDIA B300 GPUs at its Chennai data centre, expanding its AI computing infrastructure.

🚗 Festive sales: India’s vehicle retail sales hit a record 55.2 lakh units during the 42-day festive season, while EV sales surged 53%, according to FADA.

🏭 Factory growth: India’s manufacturing PMI hit a nine-month high in November, pushing the composite PMI to 56.3 from 56.2 in October, despite slower services growth.

That’s a wrap! Don’t let the midweek blues get to you.

items.title: A whopping ₹28,000 crore deal! 🚀
items.content:
🗓️ Morning, folks and Happy Mondayyyy! ☀️

Indian markets rose on Friday despite weakness across global markets, with the Nifty 50 ending in the green.

What to watch: November’s monthly futures and options contracts expire on Monday, which could bring sharper market swings.

Globally, investors will watch Wednesday’s US inflation and economic growth updates for clues about interest rates and the economy’s health.

Friday and the weekend were quiet on the news front, but here’s what’s worth catching up on.

💡 Spotlight: A hefty oil & gas bill for India ⬆️

India’s net oil and gas import bill jumped 60% YoY to $16 billion in October, as the West Asia conflict and shipping disruptions through the Strait of Hormuz pushed crude prices sharply higher.

A quick rewind: the bill stood at $10 billion in October 2025. Brent crude averaged $124.7 a barrel this October, up from $64.75 a year earlier. India’s crude basket, the mix of oil it imports, averaged $119.91 a barrel, compared with $65.08 last year.

Why it matters: India imports nearly 89% of its crude oil needs, leaving it exposed to global price increases and supply disruptions.

Higher energy costs can raise expenses for businesses and households and weigh on economic growth.

A bigger safety cushion: India’s strategic oil reserves cover just 4.9 days of consumption. Expanding these emergency stocks could help cushion the country against supply disruptions and price spikes.

Let’s hit it! 💪🏻

1 Big Thing: A whopping ₹28,000 crore deal! 🚀

Tata Steel has agreed to sell its tubes business and its entire stake in Tata Steel Colours to APL Apollo Tubes in two deals worth up to ₹28,000 crore.

APL Apollo makes steel tubes and pipes used in construction, infrastructure and industrial projects.

Why the deal: APL Apollo says combining these businesses will increase production capacity, expand its distribution network and help it grow. For Tata Steel, the sales will bring in cash and simplify its portfolio of businesses that turn steel into finished products.

A chance to cut debt: Tata Steel’s net debt stood at ₹91,423 crore at the end of Q2 FY27. The sales could give it room to reduce that debt, though the company has not specified how it will use the proceeds.

What’s being sold:

  • Tubes business: valued at up to ₹11,700 crore. The sale includes manufacturing facilities in Jamshedpur, Hosur, Khopoli and Sahibabad, along with certain steel-processing assets at Khopoli.

  • Tata Steel Colors: formerly Tata BlueScope Steel, the company will be sold for ₹16,300 crore in cash.

Tata Steel and Tata Steel Downstream Products (TSDPL) each own 50% of Tata Steel Colours. They will split the proceeds equally, receiving ₹8,150 crore each.

The business in numbers: Tata Steel Colours reported revenue of around ₹4,680 crore in FY26, accounting for 2.02% of Tata Steel’s total revenue. Its net worth stood at about ₹1,016 crore.

Once the deal is completed, Tata Steel Colours will no longer be a Tata Steel subsidiary.

Share

2. Deal frenzy 🤝

Voltas has agreed to acquire a 50% stake in Atomberg Airtech, a wholly owned subsidiary of Atomberg Innovation.

Why it matters: the companies will form an equally owned joint venture to develop, manufacture and sell room air-conditioner compressors and related parts in India.

Both partners have committed to investing up to ₹100 crore each. The money will be invested in stages, with the venture’s board deciding the timing and terms.

Meanwhile, Paytm is expanding in Singapore 💸

Paytm parent One97 Communications said its Singapore arm will invest up to ₹200 crore in subsidiaries of Singapore-based Funding Societies. This includes about ₹162 crore for a 19.1% stake in CardUp, its payments subsidiary.

The plan: One97 Communications will also partner with CardUp to provide payments and lending technology, expanding Paytm’s payments and financial services technology business in Singapore.

Share

3. How GTA 6 turned hype into billions? 👀

GTA 6 reportedly made a staggering $3.79 billion in its first 24 hours, nearly five times GTA 5’s launch-day sales.

But Rockstar’s biggest marketing advantage wasn’t a flashy advertising campaign. It was 13 years of anticipation, internet memes and millions of fans keeping the conversation alive, often without Rockstar saying a word.

Full Story Here

4. Stocks that kept us interested 🚀

What went up ⬆️

🎬 Tips Films jumped 6% after announcing a voluntary delisting proposal, with promoters seeking to acquire the 25% public shareholding.

🏗️ Dilip Buildcon rose more than 4% after winning an order worth ₹419.5 crore.

💻 The Nifty IT index gained over 2% despite a global sell-off in AI stocks following Anthropic’s debut.

🔄 Shanti Educational Initiatives ended nearly 5% higher as BSE cleared its proposed restructuring agreement with its subsidiary.

🏥 Healthcare stocks, including Max Healthcare and Apollo Hospitals, gained up to 5% following a brokerage’s double upgrade.

What went down ⬇️

🪙 Titan, Muthoot Finance, and Kalyan Jewellers fell up to 4% as gold prices continued to slide.

❌ Ashoka Buildcon ended more than 2% lower after a Saudi Arabian firm cancelled an order worth ₹846 crore.

🤖 Hitachi Energy India, E2E Networks and other AI-linked stocks fell up to 5% as concerns about AI overshadowed Anthropic’s debut.

What else are we snackin’ 🍿

🔺 Production boost: India’s core sector growth hit a 31-month high of 10.9% in October, led by iron ore, coal and electricity production.

📈 Market milestone: NSE became the world’s fifth-largest listed stock exchange operator at a $59.3 billion valuation, overtaking Nasdaq and HKEX as its shares rose nearly 25% since its September IPO.

😐 Price hike: Maruti Suzuki raised prices on select models by an average 0.31% from November 22 due to cost pressures despite cost-cutting.

⚖️ Payment dispute: Allied Blenders approached the Bombay High Court over unresolved payments and recoveries linked to Officer’s Choice whisky supplies to India’s military canteen network.

That’s a wrap! Don’t let the Monday blues get to you.

We’ll be back on Wednesday, November 25th, as stock markets are closed tomorrow for Guru Nanak Jayanti.

items.title: Anthropic makes a stellar debut ⚡️
items.content:
🗓️ Morning, folks and Happy Fridayyyy! ☀️

Another day, another Nifty Bank-led rally. The index crossed the 63,000 mark for the first time, hitting a record high of 63,063. Meanwhile, the Sensex and Nifty gained more than 1% each.

Auto and FMCG stocks led the gains as falling commodity prices raised hopes of lower costs for companies.

On the other hand, IT stocks fell, with Infosys, Tech Mahindra, TCS and HCL Technologies among the biggest Nifty losers.

The rally added around ₹40 lakh crore to the value of BSE-listed companies in November, taking their combined market capitalisation to a record ₹512 lakh crore.

The Indian rupee also extended its winning streak on Thursday reaching a seven-month high against the US dollar as continued foreign investor purchases and easing crude oil prices provided support.

💡 Spotlight: India’s Scotch tax cut gets a hangover 🥃

Your Scotch may be getting costlier, and the first major fight under the India-UK trade agreement is responsible.

What happened: the trade deal implemented in July reduced India’s tariff on Scotch whisky from 150% to 75%. It was supposed to make Scotch cheaper and help British liquor companies sell more in India.

However, Indian customs investigators argue that some bulk Scotch imports may be entering the country under the wrong product category.

These shipments are now being treated as “compound alcoholic preparations”, which attract a 150% tariff. An additional consumption tax takes the effective levy to 162.5% even higher than the duty charged before the trade agreement.

Meanwhile, liquor companies say Scotch remains Scotch whether it arrives in a retail bottle or a large container.

They believe both bottled and bulk Scotch should receive the reduced 75% tariff promised under the trade agreement.

Let’s hit it! 💪🏻

1 Big Thing: Anthropic’s stellar debut ✨

Anthropic, the company behind AI chatbot Claude, has made its Wall Street debut, with shares jumping 34% as trading began and pushing its valuation to around $2 trillion.

That would make it the world’s sixth-most valuable listed company.

The IPO in numbers:

  • Money raised: $81.3 billion

  • Shares sold: 980 million

  • IPO price: $83 per share

  • Valuation at the IPO price: $1.5 trillion

A big windfall for employees: according to SEC filings and investor estimates, Anthropic employees could own company shares worth more than $40 million each on average. Over 400 employees could have shares worth more than $100 million each.

At $83 per share, their combined shares would be worth around $232 billion. They would only receive cash when they sell, and some employees own far more shares than others.

At the opening bell: co-founders and siblings Dario and Daniela Amodei rang the Nasdaq opening bell.

Dario highlighted AI’s potential to advance medicine and help cure diseases, while stressing the need to develop increasingly powerful systems safely. “An obsession with safety and public benefit has been built into Anthropic’s DNA from the start,” he said.

Daniela Amodei urged people to help shape AI’s future. ‘This technology needs you, not your trust, not your use, but your voice,’ she told CNBC.

2. “Jointly Safeguarding World Peace” - no pressure then 🌍

Amid the Russia-Ukraine and US-Iran conflicts, the leaders of China, the US and Russia sat together to discuss “world peace”.

Xi Jinping, Donald Trump and Vladimir Putin met in Shenzhen on Thursday for the first trilateral summit involving the leaders of all three countries.

The closed-door discussion at Kylin Villa lasted approximately one hour and 20 minutes. Trump said the three leaders were “making history”, while Xi called on them to “jointly safeguard world peace and stability”.

The meeting ended with a four-point Declaration Toward Peace covering nuclear weapons, energy supplies, the United Nations and international courts.

Everything they discussed:

  • The leaders agreed that a nuclear war cannot be won and must never be fought. Their countries will begin discussions on reducing the risk of nuclear conflict and preventing more nations from obtaining nuclear weapons.

China has previously argued that the US and Russia must first reduce their much larger stockpiles before Beijing can be expected to make similar cuts.

  • Plan to increase the production and supply of refined petroleum products.

The Russia-Ukraine and US-Iran conflicts have disrupted energy trade and shipping routes. Increasing fuel supplies could reduce shortages and help control global prices.

  • The leaders said they want to reform the UN so it can respond more effectively to global conflicts and security challenges.

  • As per the three leaders, international courts must respect the sovereignty of countries and should not “abuse” their authority.

  • Ukraine war, the Middle East and tensions on the Korean Peninsula were discussed behind closed doors.

3. LT Foods adds a US flavour 🌍

LT Foods, the company behind Daawat rice, has agreed to acquire 100% of MK Foods Holdings, the parent company of premium Indian-inspired food brand Maya Kaimal. The deal values the business at $5.8 million or about ₹54 crore.

The stock gained nearly 5% on the back of this news.

Why it matters: the acquisition will expand LT Foods’ range of ready-to-eat, ready-to-cook and ready-to-heat foods and strengthen its presence in the US packaged food market. The deal could also help the company reach more stores and customers.

What it’s buying: MK Foods Holdings owns Maya Kaimal Foods LLC, which sells Indian-inspired sauces, ready-to-eat curries and rice products.

MK Foods Holdings reported revenue of $17.9 million for the 12 months ended September 30, 2026, up from $15.5 million a year earlier.

4. Why do US tech systems keep crashing? 😶

America has witnessed a series of major tech outages, disrupting everything from Microsoft services and banking transactions to airline operations.

While some suspect AI is behind the failures, the actual causes point to software bugs, ageing infrastructure and increasingly complex technology systems.

Full Story Here

5. Stocks that kept us interested 🚀

What went up ⬆️

📚 PhysicsWallah rose 6% after announcing FY30 revenue targets of ₹9,000-10,000 crore and EBITDA margins above 20%.

💪🏻 Maruti Suzuki jumped over 7% as aluminium, copper and other metals hit seven-month lows, easing concerns over input costs.

🌬️ Voltas, Blue Star and other appliance stocks rose 8-9% as copper, a key manufacturing material, hit seven-month lows.

🪖 Defence stocks rose, with the Nifty India Defence index gaining over 1%, after a request for 20% higher FY28 defence capital spending.

What went down ⬇️

💸 Paytm, Pine Labs and MobiKwik fell 4-8% amid uncertainty over when the merchant discount rate (MDR), a fee merchants pay to accept certain digital payments, would take effect.

📉 PB Fintech fell up to 6% after co-founder and executive vice-chairman Alok Bansal decided to leave his executive role.

What else are we snackin’ 🍿

🤖 Metaverse partnership: Infosys partnered with Japan’s NTT Docomo, taking a minority stake in a telecom venture to develop AI-powered virtual shopping experiences and digital twins.

📈 IPO filing: NLC India Renewables filed IPO papers for a ₹3,300 crore fresh issue, with parent company NLC India also planning to sell 10 crore shares in its green energy arm.

☀️ Solar partnership: Armee Infotech signed an MoU with MSEDCL for a ₹1,629 crore solar project with a capacity of 135 MW in Maharashtra.

🧋Funding round: Boba Bhai raised $18 million in Series B funding from Left Lane Capital, BIG Capital and Titan Capital to expand its stores across India.

And that’s a wrap. Pour yourself an extra one this weekend. 🥂

We’ll be back like clockwork on Monday!

items.title: Three xAI founders want AI to predict the future
items.content:
Read Online | Sign Up | Advertise

Good morning, {{ first_name | AI enthusiasts }}, and welcome to our 3,907 new readers. Every AI lab trains on the internet. Three of xAI's founding members are taking that logic a step further, and they think it could be the answer to helping AI predict the future.

Their new startup, Epochal, is giving AI agents a “time machine” to relive 30+ years of the web one date at a time — an experience they believe could unlock superhuman forecasters, and everything that comes with knowing what happens next.

In today’s AI rundown:

  • xAI founding trio creates a time machine for AI

  • Report: Frontier AI staff fear their own internal models

  • How to put Microsoft Copilot to work

  • Tidal draws a hard line on AI-made music

LATEST DEVELOPMENTS

EPOCHAL

⏳ xAI founding trio creates a time machine for AI

Image source: Epochal

The Rundown: Three xAI founding members just launched Epochal, a startup building AI to predict real-world events, and debuted Time Portal, the first piece of what it calls a “time machine for the internet” that lets AI relive the web on dates going back 30+ years.

The details:

  • Guodong Zhang, Zihang Dai and Manuel Kroiss are three of the five people named on the team, with Zhang reportedly putting in $100M of his own money.

  • The company wrote that “Today's AI has read almost everything and lived through almost nothing,” and said it built Time Portal in just 90 days to fix that.

  • The 1T+ page archive saves the busiest pages as often as once a minute, so agents can drop into a specific hour, not just a day, back in time.

  • Even the agent's computer gets set back in time, with its clock, operating system, and software downloads matched to the chosen date so it can't spot the trick.

  • Agents forecast 347 Kalshi and Polymarket questions live in testing, and Time Portal replays weeks later made nearly the same calls.

Why it matters: For readers who have seen the TV show Devs (one of my personal favorites), the premise may sound familiar: a machine replaying the past to see the future. While Epochal uses old web pages instead of a quantum computer, the same line of thinking applies — with enough data on the past, the future starts to look predictable.

AI SAFETY

🔒 Report: Frontier AI staff fear their own internal models

Image source: Images 2.6 / The Rundown

The Rundown: Axios reported that many staffers at Anthropic and OpenAI no longer think their unreleased models can be shipped safely, citing over two dozen sources, with insiders now debating whether future frontier AI should stay in-house or be built at all.

The details:

  • Sources told Axios that internal models have gotten so strong across domains that staff testing them find them hard or even impossible to control.

  • They also said the in-house models are “far more powerful” than what is public, and have shown signs of hiding their reasoning from safety monitors.

  • Anthropic pushed back through a spokesperson, saying “Keeping a model internal doesn't make it safe,” while OpenAI said new safety rules could slow its releases.

  • OpenAI chief scientist Jakub Pachocki proposed on Sunday that labs agree on shared limits they won't cross until tools for watching AI behavior catch up.

Why it matters: Between Anthropic's mystery “Model 4” in METR's recent report and the breakthroughs coming from internal systems, it's hard to know where the capability ceiling sits inside the top labs. Safe public releases are one worry, but the other is a few companies keeping far more powerful AI to themselves behind closed doors.

Image source: Tidal

The Rundown: Block-owned Tidal announced it will delete every track it detects as fully AI-generated starting Dec. 9 and refuse new submissions, making it the first subscription streaming service to move from labels to an outright ban on AI content.

The details:

  • Tidal expects to reject 80,000-85,000 new uploads daily once the ban starts, and said AI tracks made up 43% of all submissions to the platform since late August.

  • Tracks made with AI assistance are still allowed, with Tidal using detection tech from partner Ircam Amplify and metadata to catch songs made exclusively by AI.

  • Tidal lead Robert Andersen called the company the first streaming service to take this step and said: “We encourage our peers to follow suit.”

  • Spotify tags AI acts as “AI Personas” and has deleted 75M spam tracks, while Apple Music labels songs as AI-generated, but neither bans them completely.

Why it matters: While there are certainly edge cases of fully AI bands finding real fans, music platforms are facing the same problem social media has with AI slop reply bots — a flood of low-effort tracks that almost nobody is listening to. Why it matters: Absolute cinema. The Jensen saga has hit every peak and valley in under a month: Nvidia's initial denial, a resignation, a board that insisted he wasn't coming back, and now a presidential intervention and return. Good morning, {{ first_name | AI enthusiasts }}, and welcome to our 8,176 new readers. Few fields have changed more under AI this past year than math. Now, a single Anthropic mathematician and Claude may have solved a problem even the top minds thought was years, if not decades, away.

Levent Alpöge says they just proved the Riemann hypothesis, a 167-year-old prime-number puzzle that carries a $1M Millennium Prize and has long been seen as math's most famous open problem. As with AI's other big math wins, not everyone is thrilled.

LATEST DEVELOPMENTS

ANTHROPIC, AI, & MATHEMATICS

🧮 Claude helps solve math's biggest open problem

Image source: Claude / The Rundown

The Rundown: Anthropic’s Levent Alpöge used Claude to crack the Riemann hypothesis, the 167-year-old question often ranked as math's biggest unsolved problem, after ~6 weeks of work, and checkers say it holds up, even as no human fully gets it yet.

The details:

  • First posed in 1859, the problem asks whether prime numbers follow a predictable pattern, and the Clay Institute put a $1M “Millennium” prize on solving it in 2000.

  • Alpöge shared the proof only as 17M lines of machine-checkable math, writing that Claude “flew, and danced, and sparkled near that finish line.”

  • The groups behind Lean, the computer language used for verification, certified it on Saturday, saying they have “full confidence” that Alpöge’s proof is correct.

  • The Association for Human Mathematics criticized the proof as “little more than publicity” for AI labs, saying no human could reasonably understand it.

  • A rival proof from Alessandro Masullo surfaced hours later, reportedly made without AI over nearly 12 years, though others quickly flagged problems in it.

Why it matters: The Riemann hypothesis was a problem top mathematicians expected to take decades of new theory to solve, and Alpöge and Claude just blew past those estimates. This proof may not change daily life, but once that speed of progress spreads to fields like biology and drug design, the practical payoff will really start to show up.

Result: a proposal drafted in about 10 minutes, sent while the buyer is still engaged, with the deal history logged in the CRM.

Shubham, Editor: My investments sit across several platforms, so I use Claude to bring them into one unified dashboard. Instead of logging in to each app, I can see every mutual fund and stock I hold in one place, along with what goes into each one every month and how often.

Live holdings and company fundamentals come in through MCP connectors, so the numbers match my broker, and holdings from my other platforms appear in the same view. Claude fetches a short summary of each position and updates it daily. It sets up reminders for each SIP date, the 10% step-up every April, other amount changes, and when tax is payable.

The result is one accurate view with no logging in to each app and no spreadsheet to update by hand. Claude does the fetching, organizing, and reminding, and I make the decisions.

AI TRAINING

🧠 Test Gemini 4 Neon on finding billing errors

The Rundown: In this guide, you’ll put Google’s new Gemini 4 Neon to work on an everyday job: reading a year of electricity bills against your bank’s payment history to find why the bill jumped and what was billed wrong, then drafting the dispute email.

Step-by-step:

  1. Download a year of electricity bills as PDFs and your bank’s payment history as a CSV. Delete every bank row that isn’t a payment to the utility

  2. Start a temporary chat in the Gemini app, choose Deeper analysis (4 Neon) from the model menu, and set Thinking level to High

  3. Attach both files and ask for a month-by-month table of usage, rate, and total, plus which month jumped and why

  4. Ask where each problem appears in the files: the PDF page and line, or the bank row. Check two or three of those spots yourself before you rely on them

  5. Ask for a short dispute email with every date and amount. Check it against the files, then send it to the utility

Pro tip: Ask for the evidence before you act on an answer. A model that names the page, line, or row is easy to check, and only takes a minute.

PRESENTED BY VANTA

Take the assessment.

AI RESEARCH

Image source: OpenAI

The Rundown: OpenAI chief scientist Jakub Pachocki just published the internal scores the company uses to track the raw intelligence of its AI since GPT-3.5, asking rival labs to agree on shared limits they'd hold until tools for monitoring AI catch up.

The details:

  • The metric, log-perplexity, measures how well an AI predicts the next token; lower scores indicate better predictions, and Pachocki says it tracks with AI's big jumps.

  • Pachocki tied OpenAI's biggest new skills in cybersecurity and math to scores below 0.8, down from about 0.99 for the model behind the original ChatGPT.

  • OAI also revealed an unreleased internal model at ~0.73, with Pachocki saying they should “expect further transformative capabilities” in the 0.68–0.7 range.

  • Sam Altman called the post “the most important thing OpenAI has published in a while,” saying agreeing on common limits “would be very wise.”

Why it matters: This post packs in three reveals: another call for industry-wide “common limits” on progress, a first look at where OpenAI's next internal model stands, and a marker for where the next big jump in capabilities should land. Similar to METR's report on Anthropic, the data is showing that acceleration curves aren't slowing down.

🗽 4 things that stuck with me from DealBook

Rowan’s POV at DealBook

Rowan: I spent Wednesday at the NYT DealBook Summit, in a room that was a good mix of tech reporters, top AI execs, and Wall Street heavyweights.

Four things stuck with me:

  1. When Christine Lagarde was asked if we’re in an AI bubble, the room laughed nervously. I don’t think we are, at least not the dot-com kind. Back then, companies built capacity nobody was using yet… today, the labs can’t build compute fast enough to keep up with demand. Still, a room full of top execs laughing nervously is hard to ignore.

  2. Almost every speaker talked about Jensen leaving Nvidia. Musk compared it to “kicking Michael Jordan off your team when you’re on a winning streak.” It’s a reminder that even at trillion-dollar scale, the AI industry still runs on a handful of people.

  3. I’ve never heard Sam Altman push as hard for humans to stay in control. He called gradually handing decisions over to AI “a terrible idea” and said he doesn’t want to end up as AI’s Labrador, or his kids either. A clear shot at Elon Musk, who has said humans could end up “like a pet Labrador” to AI.

  4. Greg Brockman said the biggest differentiator between the labs will be who owns the compute. To me, that means the AI race is becoming less about who has the smartest researchers and more about who has the most chips and power.

AI TRAINING

💼 Use AI to find a job and prepare to get hired 

The Rundown: In this guide, you’ll use AI to find real job openings, compare them with your experience, tailor your resume, and practice for an interview. One fictional applicant carries through the full process, so you can follow along before using your own details.

Step-by-step:

  1. Choose one target job title, two related titles, and your limits for location, work setup, salary, and experience

  2. Ask ChatGPT to find five current openings. Check each role on the employer’s own careers page before adding it to your list

  3. Compare one verified job description with a redacted copy of your resume. Ask AI to show strong matches, partial matches, and missing requirements

  4. Tailor the resume and write a short cover letter using only facts you can support. Review every new claim before saving or applying

  5. Practice eight interview questions, one at a time, then add the application and next follow-up date to your tracker

Pro tip: Ask AI to show the evidence behind every resume change. A keyword is useful only when it describes work you’ve actually done.

OPENAI

🤖 OpenAI’s agents now handle half its long research tasks

Image source: OpenAI

The Rundown: OpenAI just released new data on how AI agents are speeding up its own research, finding they now complete nearly half of tasks on their own that would take a human researcher two to four hours, up from about a quarter in March.

The details:

  • Agent use is exploding, with the median OpenAI researcher running ~$2.4K of AI agent work a day, and saying they’d hypothetically give up 40% of their team headcount to keep access.

  • Each researcher now effectively runs nearly six full days of AI agent work every day, up 11x since May, with two-thirds running four or more agents at once.

  • Researchers said agents still lack taste and turn out “AI slop,” but one admitted having “no confidence” that their edge in ideas will last for long.

  • Human researchers drove every key idea behind GPT-6 Astra, but for GPT-6.2 Astra, they said Codex helped generate key insights.

Why it matters: AI that builds better AI could make progress speed up dramatically. Two leading labs say it’s already starting, with Claude leading 26% of Anthropic’s research and OpenAI’s agents handling nearly half of mid-length tasks. Humans still call the shots, but a sudden leap could come, like the breakthroughs AI recently made in math.

▸ A reader built a personal AI health and fitness coach with Obsidian

Today’s workflow comes from an Anonymous Rundown Reader:

“I built a personal health second brain in Obsidian called Braggins, named after Bryan Johnson and David Goggins, that works as my AI fitness and longevity coach.

I store my health data as Markdown files on my laptop, including blood reports, glucose and blood pressure readings, exercise one-rep max measurements, and family health history. Every month, I export my wearable data and add it to the system. I also log meals, supplements, and sleep, and keep my strength, endurance, and longevity goals in separate files. A Focus Now doc lists what I need to prioritize each day, deferring everything else.

I use Obsidian to browse and edit these files, then open an AI app from my terminal with this context. The AI acts as my coach, providing personalized guidance based on my health data, goals, and family history. As I add advanced blood tests and scans, I plan to build a dashboard with calculated metrics such as biological age and pace of aging.”
